passage:
"...so if we sort the vendor list by delivery time, then the whole—" said Elizabeth.
Sachin glanced at the phone in his hand. "Hmm. Sorry, gotta run." He was gone.
Elizabeth stood in the corridor with the sentence unfinished. "Oh. Okay," she said to nobody, and told Neha at the next desk, "It felt like being switched off mid-word."
"Ouch," said Neha.
The next morning Sachin stopped at Elizabeth's desk. "About yesterday. I cut you off, and I'm sorry. I had to take a call. Can I hear the rest of your idea at three?"
Elizabeth looked up. "Three's fine."
"Good. I really want to hear it."
The knot in her chest loosened.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth saying when Sachin glanced at his phone?
qa.a: That if the vendor list is sorted by delivery time, then the whole plan could change.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth feel when Sachin left in the middle of her sentence?
qa.a: Dismissed, as if switched off mid-word. Elizabeth stood in the corridor with the sentence unfinished and spoke of it to Neha.

qa.q: What did Sachin do the next morning that softened the sting?
qa.a: Sachin apologised for cutting Elizabeth off, gave the reason, and asked to hear the rest at three.

qa.q: Why might Sachin have glanced at the phone and hurried away?
qa.a: Because of a call that Sachin had to take. Sachin later said so, but the missing explanation at the time left Elizabeth to guess.

grounding: Elizabeth feels dismissed when Sachin ends a chat mid-thought after glancing at a phone, and a promise to continue softens it.

passage:
My name is Neelam. Last month at the coffee counter I was halfway through explaining a client's request when Bhupen looked down at his phone and said, "Right, later," and walked off. Nothing terrible. Still, I felt small, as if my sentence hadn't been worth finishing. I drank the coffee cold.
A week later it happened again. His phone lit up while I was talking. But this time Bhupen raised a hand and said, "I need to take this. Hold that thought, I really want to hear it. Four o'clock?" I said yes. The phone was the same and the interruption was the same, but I felt nothing like the first time.

qa.q: What did Bhupen say the first time before walking off?
qa.a: "Right, later."

qa.q: How did Neelam feel after the first cut-off, and what shows it?
qa.a: Small and dismissed. Neelam felt the sentence was not worth finishing and drank the coffee cold.

qa.q: What did Bhupen change the second time?
qa.a: Bhupen raised a hand, said the call had to be taken, asked Neelam to hold the thought and suggested four o'clock.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have seen the first cut-off?
qa.a: Possibly as a quick "later" that did not seem serious, unaware that Neelam felt small; the second time Bhupen showed the closing mattered.

grounding: Neelam feels dismissed when Bhupen cuts off a chat after a phone glance, and a promise to continue later softens it.

passage: In the office break room, Vikas was halfway through explaining his idea for the new client report to Chaitanya. "So if we split the data by region first, then—" Chaitanya glanced at his phone, said "Yeah, sounds good, got to go," and walked out. Vikas stood by the kettle, face hot. He felt stupid for being so excited. For the next hour he didn't say a word to anyone. At four, a message popped up: "Sorry I cut you off. My manager had just pinged me. I actually want to hear the region idea properly. 5 minutes after the standup tomorrow?" Vikas read it twice. His shoulders loosened. He typed back, "Sure. I'll bring the sketch." The next morning Chaitanya listened to the whole thing and asked two questions.

qa.q: What was Vikas's idea about?
qa.a: Splitting the data for the new client report by region first.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel when Chaitanya walked out?
qa.a: He felt dismissed and embarrassed, his face hot, feeling stupid for being so excited.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya do that softened the sting?
qa.a: He apologised, explained the reason and set a specific time to hear the rest, showing he truly wanted to continue.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya seem to feel after cutting Vikas off?
qa.a: He seemed a bit regretful, sending a sorry message and listening fully the next day.

grounding: Shows a person feeling dismissed when a colleague ends a chat abruptly, and how a promise to continue softens the sting.

passage:
Subject: Our chat yesterday

Hi Sabina,

I wanted to say thanks for your message last night. Honestly, when you glanced at your phone and said "gotta run" while I was halfway through telling you about the vendor problem, I felt a bit brushed off. I went back to my desk thinking maybe I'd been boring you.

Then your text came: "Sorry, got called into a meeting, I really want to hear the rest. Tomorrow at 10?" That made a huge difference. I didn't feel dismissed anymore.

So see you at 10. I'll bring the numbers.

And for what it's worth, I've started doing the same thing when I have to rush off. It's a small habit, but it helps.

Manoj

qa.q: When did Sabina suggest they continue?
qa.a: Tomorrow at 10.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel when Sabina left mid-conversation?
qa.a: Manoj felt a bit brushed off, wondering if the story had been boring.

qa.q: What small habit is Manoj copying from Sabina, and why is it helpful?
qa.a: Following a sudden exit with a quick promise to continue later, which stops the other person feeling dismissed.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel reading this email?
qa.a: Sabina would probably feel glad the message helped, and appreciated for making the effort.

grounding: Shows a person feeling dismissed when a colleague cuts a chat short with a glance at the phone, and how a promise to continue softens it.

passage:
"Akka, you asked why I was quiet at dinner. I'm Lakshmi, your sister, and I'm going to overthink this out loud, okay?
Today at work, I was telling Ujjwal about the problem with the new schedule. I'd been thinking about it all week. Halfway through my sentence, he looked at his phone, said 'Okay, cool,' and walked off. Just like that.
I stood there feeling like I'd been talking to a wall. I kept thinking, was I boring? Does he not respect me?
Then an hour later, he came back to my desk. He said, 'Sorry, I cut you off. My daughter's school called. Can you tell me the rest now?' And he actually listened.
It's funny. The cut-off stung so much. But that one sentence afterwards fixed most of it."

qa.q: What did Ujjwal say when he came back to Lakshmi's desk?
qa.a: He said, 'Sorry, I cut you off. My daughter's school called. Can you tell me the rest now?'

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel when Ujjwal walked off?
qa.a: She felt dismissed and hurt, like talking to a wall, wondering if she was boring or not respected.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do that softened the sting?
qa.a: He came back, apologised, explained the reason and asked to hear the rest, then listened.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt about cutting Lakshmi off?
qa.a: He probably felt a bit sorry, which is why he came back to apologise and listen.

grounding: Shows a person feeling dismissed when a colleague ends a chat mid-thought, and how an apology and promise to continue soften it.

passage:
Monday. Yogesh was halfway through his idea for the client dashboard when Tejas glanced at his phone, said, "Okay, cool," and walked off. Yogesh stood in the corridor holding his half-sentence. He spent the afternoon wondering if the idea was stupid.
Wednesday. Tejas did it again at the coffee machine. This time Yogesh felt his jaw tighten, and he didn't bring the idea up at the stand-up.
Friday. Tejas's phone buzzed mid-conversation. He looked at it, then back at Yogesh. "Sorry, it's the client, I have to take this. I want to hear the rest, though. Four o'clock?" At four he came to Yogesh's desk with two cups of tea. Yogesh noticed how different the same interruption felt.

qa.q: What time did Tejas suggest on Friday?
qa.a: He suggested four o'clock.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel after Monday's cut-off?
qa.a: He felt dismissed and unsure, left holding his half-sentence and wondering all afternoon if the idea was stupid.

qa.q: What changed on Friday that softened the interruption?
qa.a: Tejas gave a reason, said he wanted to hear the rest, named a time and came back with tea.

qa.q: What might Tejas not have realised on Monday and Wednesday?
qa.a: He may not have noticed that his quick "Okay, cool" left Yogesh feeling his idea didn't matter.

grounding: Shows a person feeling dismissed when a colleague ends a chat mid-thought with a glance at his phone, and how a promise to continue softens it.
